newsitem.title: CANADA: CRTC approves local phone competition, convergence.
newsitem.headline: CRTC approves local phone competition, convergence.

text.p: Canada's communications regulatory agency on Thursday threw the local telephone market open to competition while also promoting convergence between the phone and broadcast businesses.

A complex set of decisions by the Canadian Radio- television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) also approved a C$3 a month increase in local phone charges effective on January 1, 1998, and a price cap formula to apply to services thereafter.

The decisions, which can be appealed to the federal cabinet, opened the local phone market to competition immediately and said phone companies would be allowed to apply to begin broadcast distribution in 1998.

In a significant deviation from the route taken in the United States, the agency denied a request by companies such as Sprint Corp that established companies like BCE Inc be forced to sell local services at wholesale rates -- at a discount to the retail rate. A CRTC official explained the rationale was to force new entrants to build new infrastructure rather than merely to buy wholesale and resell.

The C$3 increase in local monthly rates, following two increases of C$2 each, were designed to more accurately reflect the cost of providing local phone services, which are subsidized by long-distance calls.
The CRTC decided that the subsidies from long-distance calls should move toward two cents per minute, with the goal that this be completed by the start of 1998.

For 1997, BCE Inc's Bell Canada has a rate of lower than two cents, but elsewhere the long-distance "contribution" was as much as four cents per minute. The higher local rates, newly "rebalanced", will enable the decline toward two cents.
Costs are particularly high for providing residential services in Canada's vast rural areas and companies will continue to be given an incentive to provide service there.
The new regime will collect long-distance subsidies or contributions in a central fund, which will reimburse companies for providing such high-cost services.

In a further decision, the CRTC decided to start requiring wireless phone companies, such as Rogers Cantel Mobil Communications Inc and BCE Mobil Communications Inc, to provide subsidies from their long-distance phone calls.

This would also apply to companies that provide cutting-edge services, such as personal communications systems (PCS) and local multipoint communications systems (LMCS), but not to paging and internet services.

A CRTC official said he did not expect this to have a major impact initially, since long-distance calls on a cell phone that go to a fixed line in a home or an office would tend to be routed through a network that would pay the subsidy already. It would apply more to calls between cell phones.
The CRTC also ensured "number portability," the concept that a subscriber can keep his number if changing companies.

It specified that each carrier providing services in the local market would be responsible for the recovery of its own local number portability costs -- that is, the costs fall on both the established and new companies.

Chairwoman Bertrand found it difficult to explain how subscribers would be better off by paying yet another monthly rate increase. But she said the increase would not be automatic, and a colleague noted that there would now be competition which would limit the tendency to raise rates. The new entrants would not have their consumer rates regulated.

She pointed out that it was important to be able to move with the advances in information technology. A CRTC official said it was conceivable that in the future only one connection would be needed to a home, providing both phone and cable services, increasingly sophisticated.
